quote: The man was Francis Bacon, his Great Idea was the scientific method, and he was the only crackpot in all history to claim that level of benefit to humanity and turn out to be completely right.
content: The essay's hedge answers most of this: "Bacon didn't singlehandedly invent science, of course, but he did contribute, and may have been the first to realize the power." What it credits Bacon with is the claim of benefit: that organized, cumulative inquiry would "feed the hungry, heal the sick." Fable grants that he "was right that organized inquiry would transform the world." Ibn al-Haytham had an experimental programme in optics. He did not have Salomon's House, the institutional vision the Royal Society took as its charter, with Bacon on the frontispiece of Sprat's History (1667). The tables of presence and absence were wrong in detail, and the prophecy of benefit was right. The benefit is the Great Idea the essay means.

quote: You’re also denying Martine Rothblatt’s founding of United Therapeutics to seek a cure for her daughter’s pulmonary hypertension. (Successfully, I might add.)
content: This is conceded. Treprostinil treats pulmonary arterial hypertension and does not cure it, and "successfully" should have been "successfully found a treatment that keeps her alive." It is a good specimen of the essay's own warning, an extra nice claim about science let through without checking. The paragraph's argument survives the correction. A mother founding a biotechnology company because she loved her daughter, and producing a drug that extends the lives of patients with a fatal disease, shows science tied to parental love, which is the claim the paragraph needs. The cure was the unneeded extra detail.

quote: Cut up your Great Thingy into smaller independent ideas, and treat them as independent.
content: This is agreed, and the independence caveat is one the essay's wording already handles. Armstrong's rule is to treat the parts as independent so that "the truth or falsity of one should not halo on the others." The independence is affective: the appeal of the labour theory of value should not transfer to the eschatology. It is not a license to multiply their likelihoods as independent evidence. Keeping track of which pieces stand or fall together, as Fable advises, is the "burdensome detail" discipline the same list prescribes. Grove et al. supply the evidence that mechanical decomposition beats holistic judgment (Grove et al. 2000), and the happy death spiral is holistic judgment going wrong.
